answer: The hierarchy of evidence ranks study designs by how well they isolate a causal effect: randomized trials sit at the top, followed by difference-in-differences, then pre-post comparisons, and cross-sectional snapshots at the bottom. Lower rungs cannot tell whether a program caused an improvement because the groups may already have differed or something else may have changed at the same time. This CAPHE lab shows the same diabetes-program data yielding four different answers depending on design, with a simple comparison overstating a 5% effect as 12%. What matters most is not the rung but identification: finding variation in treatment that separates cause from correlation.

faqs.q: Why do randomized trials rank above observational designs?
faqs.a: Randomization makes treatment and control groups comparable on average, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment. Lower-rung designs leave open that the groups already differed or that other changes occurred at the same time.

faqs.q: Can the same data give different causal answers?
faqs.a: Yes. In this lab, one county's diabetes-program data produces four different effect estimates depending on the design. A simple cross-sectional comparison suggests a 12% drop, while difference-in-differences attributes only about 3-5% to the program.

faqs.q: What is identification in causal inference?
faqs.a: Identification is the source of variation in treatment that lets analysts separate cause from correlation. The key question is not which design ranks highest but what variation identifies the causal effect in a given setting.

faqs.q: Can a strong observational study beat a weak RCT?
faqs.a: Yes. The ladder is a useful shortcut, but a well-designed observational study with a credible identification strategy can be more convincing than a poorly executed randomized trial.
